claims.text: A Pulumi blog post exists at /blog/sst-built-on-pulumi/ titled 'SST Runs on the Pulumi Engine: What It Means to Build on Pulumi', and it covers the engine mechanics behind SST's migration from CDK to Pulumi.
AWS CDK tied infrastructure to AWS.
Multi-cloud deployment with AWS CDK is nearly impossible / AWS CDK is AWS-only.
In its early days SST was built on top of AWS CDK, which allowed developers to define infrastructure using TypeScript or Python.
AWS CDK supports only TypeScript and Python (the table marks it as partial language support), while Pulumi supports any programming language.
Pulumi lets you define infrastructure in TypeScript, Python, Go, or C# and deploy across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and on-premises environments.

With CDK and CloudFormation, infrastructure code acts as a code generator producing an intermediary format (YAML or JSON) that is executed to deploy resources, so the code you write is not the code running during deployment.
Pulumi does not generate an intermediary format; infrastructure code is a first-class program executed directly during deployment.
Pulumi supports AWS, Azure, GCP, and on-prem infrastructure.
Pulumi offers real-time debugging, whereas AWS CDK debugging is hard due to CloudFormation.
Pulumi deployments are faster than AWS CDK deployments because of direct execution rather than CloudFormation.
AWS CDK relies on a CloudFormation state file while Pulumi uses Pulumi-managed state.
AWS CDK secrets management is limited to AWS Secrets Manager only, while Pulumi supports cross-cloud secrets.
Pulumi supports extensibility features such as custom providers and dynamic components.
Pulumi Insights provides improved visibility and debugging capabilities for deployments.
Pulumi Cloud Deployments provides advanced deployment workflows.

A Founding Engineer at SST said: 'With Pulumi, the deployment process feels like a natural extension of writing code - it's intuitive and powerful and capable of advanced things that traditional IaC tools can't handle.'
Pulumi Crosswalk for AWS simplifies 'day one' tasks, and an AWS guide exists at /docs/iac/guides/clouds/aws/.
An on-demand Pulumi workshop 'Getting Started with Infrastructure as Code on AWS' exists at pulumi.com/resources/getting-started-with-iac-pulumi-aws/.
Ion is the code name for SST's new deployment engine, which deploys constructs/components using Pulumi instead of CDK and CloudFormation, and once stable will be released as SST v3.
SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for its providers and deployment engine, while also bridging Terraform providers through Pulumi.
SST makes money primarily through its managed service SST Console, which is optional and includes a free tier.
SST is a framework for building modern full-stack applications on your own infrastructure.
Pulumi lets SST offer a faster, more flexible, and provider-agnostic infrastructure experience.
With CDK/CloudFormation, SST often had to resort to hacky workarounds or custom Lambda functions to achieve desired customization.
With Pulumi, the SST team was able to add support for new providers easily.
SST v3 replaced AWS CDK and CloudFormation with an embedded Pulumi engine that calls Terraform-bridged providers to make the underlying cloud API calls when running `sst deploy`.
Running `sst deploy` requires no separate Pulumi install and no Pulumi account or Pulumi Cloud dependency; the Pulumi engine ships inside the SST CLI.
SST v3 keeps deployment state in an S3 bucket in the user's own AWS account rather than in Pulumi Cloud.
SST v3 is the framework's Ion-based rewrite.
SST is an open source TypeScript framework, from the team formerly known as Serverless Stack, for building and deploying full-stack applications to AWS and more than 150 other providers.
SST users define app infrastructure and code together in a single `sst.config.ts` file using SST's own components, and `sst deploy` handles provisioning end to end.
Through 2023, SST's provisioning layer was built directly on AWS CDK and CloudFormation.
In late 2023 the SST team began a rewrite code-named Ion that replaced the entire deployment layer.
Ion shipped as SST v3 in mid-2024 and has been the only supported SST architecture since.
The SST team has said repeatedly, since the rewrite shipped, that SST is built on the Pulumi engine.

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "Ion is a code name for a new engine for deploying SST applications. The constructs (or components) are defined using Terraform providers and deployed using Pulumi; as opposed to CDK and CloudFormation (CFN)."

SST's blog post 'Moving away from CDK' says: "When you run `sst deploy`, those resources make a call to an embedded Pulumi engine that makes a call to their bridged Terraform provider, and this makes the AWS SDK calls to create your resources."
The SST docs page 'What is SST' says: "SST uses Pulumi behind the scenes for the providers and the deployment engine. And Terraform's providers are bridged through Pulumi."

Gautier Blandin, in 'Terraform, Pulumi, SST: a tradeoff analysis', writes: "SST uses the Pulumi engine under the hood to manage and provision resources, and lets users write Pulumi code in addition to using SST's constructs, enabling resources with no associated SST constructs to still be defined and deployed."
Kiryl Anoshka, in 'SST ditches AWS CDK. Time to move on to Ion', writes: "You may notice right away the imports from Pulumi. It means the whole deployment process will be built on Pulumi now."

The published `platform/package.json` for SST's platform package depends on `@pulumi/pulumi`, plus first-party Pulumi providers for AWS, Cloudflare, Docker builds and more, alongside a Pulumiverse Vercel provider (`@pulumi/aws`, `@pulumi/cloudflare`, `@pulumi/command`, `@pulumi/docker-build`, `@pulumi/random`, `@pulumi/tls`, `@pulumiverse/vercel`).
The SST repository is `anomalyco/sst`, formerly `sst/sst`.

In SST's deploy chain, SST reads `sst.config.ts` and resolves components, compiling them into Pulumi resource declarations; the Pulumi engine diffs desired vs. actual state, builds a dependency graph, and orders operations; Terraform-bridged providers translate each resource into cloud API calls via Pulumi's Terraform bridge.
Pulumi's engine provides dependency resolution, preview and diff, state tracking, and plumbing to hundreds of provider APIs.
AWS alone exposes hundreds of resource types, each with its own create, update, and delete semantics.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge (pulumi/pulumi-terraform-bridge) is Apache-2.0 licensed.
Pulumi's Terraform bridge was built specifically to let projects like SST reuse Terraform's ecosystem of providers, adapted for the Pulumi engine.
Pulumi's engine can run without a Pulumi account, a network call to Pulumi Cloud, or any Pulumi-hosted service.
Pulumi's Automation API allows teams to embed Pulumi programs inside their own tools in the same way SST embeds the engine.
Any Pulumi user can consume Terraform providers directly through the provider bridge.
The cross-referenced blog post 'Introducing: Support For Using Any Terraform Provider with Pulumi' exists at /blog/any-terraform-provider/ and describes the bridge SST and others build on.
Nitric is a cloud-agnostic application framework that runs application deployments through the Pulumi engine.
Nitric's docs state that "all of the direct deployment providers use Pulumi under the hood for their deployments."
Official Nitric providers are built directly on Pulumi's AWS, GCP, and Azure providers.
Defang deploys Docker Compose applications to the cloud and runs deployments through the Pulumi engine via its Pulumi provider.
The Defang Pulumi provider README describes it as taking "a Compose file, translates it to a Pulumi program, and runs `pulumi up`" to provision the result.
Nitric, Defang, and SST all expose a narrower, more opinionated interface while relying on the Pulumi engine and its provider bridge underneath.
Most SST users never write a line of Pulumi code and work entirely in SST's component model.
Because SST's constructs compile to Pulumi resources, users can define resources without a dedicated SST construct directly in Pulumi and deploy them as part of the same SST app.
The latest SST release, v4.17.1, went out in July 2026.
The `sst` npm package receives roughly 796,000 downloads per week (796,291 for the week of September 5-11, 2026).
SST's team page credits the same team behind opencode, an open source AI coding agent.
The opencode GitHub repository (anomalyco/opencode) has grown quickly since launch and now has a larger GitHub following (more stars) than SST itself.
The team's attention to opencode has not changed SST's release cadence or its dependency on the Pulumi engine.
Anyone who runs SST is already running Pulumi's engine.

Pulumi Cloud provides cross-team visibility into infrastructure state, policy as code provides centrally enforceable guardrails, and Pulumi components allow sharing infrastructure patterns across an organization.
Pulumi Cloud, policy as code, and components do not require leaving the engine SST already uses.
SST's components are defined using Terraform providers bridged through the Pulumi engine; SST does not invoke the Terraform CLI or write Terraform state.
SST doesn't expose cross-team visibility, policy enforcement, or infrastructure shared across more than one application on its own.
SST is a strong fit for an opinionated full-stack application framework with infrastructure and code defined together.

Cross-referenced pages exist: /blog/aws-cdk-vs-pulumi-why-sst-switched/, /docs/iac/guides/basics/how-pulumi-works/, /docs/iac/concepts/automation-api/, /docs/iac/concepts/pulumi-cloud/, /docs/iac/concepts/policy/, /docs/iac/concepts/components/.
